questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to learn German words quickly
Why we enjoy others' bad luck, and why it may not be bad
Why celebrities often avoid paying taxes
How to behave politely when someone pushes into a supermarket queue
questions.why: They discuss schadenfreude and why that feeling 'could actually be good for us'.

questions.q: What example does Neil give to explain schadenfreude?
options: A friend who fails an exam
A footballer who misses a penalty in an important match
Someone who pushes in, then their card doesn't work
A neighbour whose car breaks down
questions.why: Neil describes someone pushing in at the supermarket whose credit card then doesn't work.

questions.q: What is Rob's first reaction to this feeling?
options: It is satisfying but also rather unkind
It is something he has never felt in his whole life
It is only felt by German people
It is completely harmless
questions.why: Rob says it is 'a very satisfying feeling – but it's quite a mean feeling too'.

questions.q: According to studies, when is this feeling especially common?
options: When the person is a close friend
When we are feeling tired
When we are in a bad mood
When it happens to someone we envy
questions.why: Rob says the feeling is normal, 'particularly when it happens to someone we envy'.

questions.q: What did psychologist Wilco Van Dijk find?
options: People only feel this joy when they are unhappy themselves
People feel it most when they think the bad luck is deserved
Children feel this emotion more than adults
The feeling is always harmful to our health
questions.why: He says people especially feel schadenfreude when they think the misfortune is deserved.

questions.q: Why does Van Dijk mention hypocrites?
options: Because their bad luck feels fair to us
Because they feel schadenfreude more than others
Because they are often on reality TV
Because they never have bad luck
questions.why: He says if hypocrites fall down, 'that also is a deserved situation'.

questions.q: What is Dr Tiffany Watt-Smith's view?
options: Schadenfreude is simply right or wrong
Moral philosophers understand our emotions better than anyone
We can feel sorry for someone and pleased at once
We should never smile at another person's problems
questions.why: She says we can commiserate with someone while a sly smile spreads across our lips.

questions.q: What does Neil joke about near the end?
options: Losing his credit card
Rob's poor German
Being a hypocrite himself, like the people in the studies
Enjoying Germany's World Cup exit
questions.why: He says he loved seeing Germany knocked out of the World Cup, then adds 'not really!'
